prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN)  -- South Africa has refused the Dalai Lama a visa to attend an international peace conference in Johannesburg this week, a presidential spokesman said. The Dalai Lama fled China in 1959 after a failed uprising against Chinese rule. The Tibetan spiritual leader and Nobel Laureate did not receive a visa because it was not in South Africa's interest for him to attend, said Thabo Masebe. South Africa thinks that, if the Dalai Lama attended the conference, the focus would shift away from the 2010 World Cup -- the global soccer championship it will host next year. "We cannot allow focus to shift to China and Tibet," Masebe said, adding that South Africa has gained much from its trading relationship with China. The Dalai Lama's fellow laureate, Archbishop Desmond Tutu, said he would boycott the event.  Watch the controversy surrounding South Africa's decision » . Former president F.W. De Klerk, another laureate, backed Tutu, saying in a statement that he would also not participate in the conference if the Dalai Lama remained excluded. De Klerk said that the decision to refuse the visa made a "mockery" of the peace conference. "The decision to exclude the Dalai Lama is irreconcilable with key principles on which our society is based including the principles of accountability, openness and responsiveness and the rights to freedom of expression and free political activity," he said. "South Africa is a sovereign constitutional democracy and should not allow other countries to dictate to it regarding who it should, and should not admit to its territory - regardless of the power and influence of the country." A representative of the Dalai Lama said he was not surprised by the decision. The Tibetan government in exile thinks that China has pressured many countries to refuse a visit by the Dalai Lama, according to Chhime Chhoekyapa, an aide in Dharamsala, India. The Dalai Lama fled China in 1959 after a failed uprising against Chinese rule. The peace conference was billed as an opportunity to showcase South Africa's role as a human-rights champion ahead of its hosting of soccer's World Cup next year. It was to bring together Noble Laureates and top soccer officials. In addition to Tutu and De Klerk, laureates Nelson Mandela and Martti Ahtisaari, Sepp Blatter, president of soccer's international governing body, and actress Charlize Theron were invited to attend. The event had the blessing of the Nobel Committee.

Invitees included Tutu, de Klerk, Nelson Mandela, Martti Ahtisaari, FIFA president Sepp Blatter, and actress Charlize Theron. The Nobel Committee had endorsed the gathering.

### Johannesburg, South Africa

Johannesburg is the largest city in South Africa and one of the country’s main economic and cultural centers. Often called “Joburg” or “Jozi,” the city grew rapidly after gold was discovered in the region in 1886. Today, it is a lively metropolis known for its diverse population, modern skyline, thriving businesses, and vibrant arts scene.

Johannesburg also has a deep connection to South Africa’s history. Important sites include the Apartheid Museum, Constitution Hill, and the nearby township of Soweto, where visitors can learn about the struggle against apartheid and the life of Nelson Mandela. With its mix of history, culture, commerce, and urban energy, Johannesburg offers a fascinating introduction to modern South Africa.

## South Africa denies Dalai Lama visa ahead of World Cup peace conference

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa** — South Africa has denied the Dalai Lama a visa to attend an international peace conference in Johannesburg, prompting criticism from Nobel laureates and accusations that the government bowed to pressure from China.

The Tibetan spiritual leader had been invited to participate in a conference intended to highlight peace, reconciliation and the role of soccer ahead of the 2010 FIFA World Cup, which South Africa was preparing to host.

Government officials said the decision was made to prevent the Dalai Lama’s visit from overshadowing preparations for the tournament.

“At this time, the focus of the world is on South Africa because of the World Cup,” a government spokesman said. “We do not want this issue to divert attention from that.”

The government denied that Beijing had dictated the decision. China considers the Dalai Lama a separatist and routinely objects when foreign governments receive him. The Dalai Lama says he seeks meaningful autonomy for Tibet, not independence.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu sharply criticized the visa refusal and said he would not attend the conference without the Dalai Lama. Former South African President F.W. de Klerk also withdrew, while organizers indicated the gathering could not proceed as planned.

Tutu, a Nobel Peace Prize winner and prominent opponent of apartheid, said the decision betrayed South Africa’s history of defending human rights.

The controversy placed the South African government in a difficult position as it sought to showcase the country’s democratic transformation ahead of the World Cup while maintaining strong economic ties with China.

Opposition parties and human rights advocates called for the decision to be reversed, arguing that a country once supported by an international anti-apartheid movement should not deny entry to a prominent advocate of nonviolence.

The Dalai Lama’s representatives expressed disappointment but said he would not seek to force the issue.

The peace conference was expected to bring together political leaders, Nobel laureates and sports figures to discuss how soccer could be used to fight racism and xenophobia. Organizers later postponed the event amid the boycott and growing dispute over the visa decision.

### South Africa’s refusal to admit the Dalai Lama

In March 2009, South Africa refused to grant the Dalai Lama a visa to attend a Johannesburg peace conference intended to highlight the country’s role in conflict resolution and promote the 2010 football World Cup. The meeting was expected to include Nobel Peace Prize laureates and other prominent figures.

### Government explanation

The government said the decision was made in South Africa’s national interest. Officials argued that the Dalai Lama’s presence would shift international attention away from South Africa and the World Cup and toward the dispute over Tibet. Government spokesman Thabo Masebe denied that Pretoria had acted under direct pressure from Beijing, although officials acknowledged that relations with China were an important consideration.

### Relationship with China

The refusal was widely interpreted as an effort to avoid offending China, which regards the Dalai Lama as a separatist despite his calls for Tibetan autonomy rather than independence. China had become one of South Africa’s most important trade and investment partners, and both countries were developing close political ties. Beijing welcomed Pretoria’s decision, reinforcing suspicions that economic and diplomatic concerns had influenced it.

### Reactions from Desmond Tutu and F.W. de Klerk

Archbishop Desmond Tutu strongly condemned the decision and withdrew from the conference in protest. He said it was disgraceful that South Africa, whose liberation struggle had benefited from international solidarity, was preventing another advocate of freedom from entering. Tutu accused the government of yielding to Chinese pressure and betraying South Africa’s human-rights principles.

Former president F.W. de Klerk also withdrew. His foundation said the exclusion of the Dalai Lama was inconsistent with the conference’s purpose and with South Africa’s stated commitment to peace, dialogue and human rights.

The controversy ultimately undermined the event, which was postponed after the withdrawals. It also fueled a broader debate over whether South Africa’s foreign policy was allowing strategic and economic ties—particularly with China—to outweigh the human-rights values embedded in its post-apartheid identity.
